title: Journal Submissions
text:
EL PASO CRIME LAB · PUBLICATIONS



EPCL publications bring together researchers, criminal justice professionals, educators, and students to examine important issues, communicate evidence, and share ideas that move the field forward.
Whether you work in criminal justice, study it, or are interested in improving it, there is a place for your contribution.
Explore our publications ↓





Four publications. Four areas of focus. One shared commitment to advancing the science and practice of criminal justice.
Select a publication to explore its subject matter and determine where your proposed contribution belongs.










01 · POLICING



Examining policing, police organizations, leadership, officer development, and evidence-based approaches to public safety.

Areas of interest
Police management · Problem-oriented policing · Organizational culture · Officer training · Crime analysis · Accountability · Police-community relationships












02 · CORRECTIONS



Examining correctional institutions, detention, incarceration, rehabilitation, reentry, and correctional administration.

Areas of interest
Institutional management · Correctional officer development · Rehabilitation · Inmate programming · Recidivism · Reentry · Correctional policy












03 · COURTS



Examining judicial administration, prosecution, defense, adjudication, and the broader administration of justice.

Areas of interest
Court efficiency · Case processing · Judicial decision-making · Diversion · Sentencing · Procedural justice · Access to justice












04 · COMMUNITY SAFETY



Examining public safety beyond traditional criminal justice institutions, including prevention, community partnerships, and local government.

Areas of interest
Crime prevention · Community interventions · Public health approaches · Neighborhood conditions · Local policy · Interagency collaboration








Our editorial philosophy
Meaningful progress requires collaboration between those who study criminal justice and those who work within it.
EPCL seeks contributions that are intellectually rigorous, accessible to professional audiences, and relevant to the communities and institutions served by the criminal justice system.





EPCL welcomes different forms of professional and scholarly contributions. You do not need to be an academic researcher or have previous publication experience.

CATEGORY 02

Emerging criminal justice issues







CATEGORY 03



Sharing professional knowledge and practical experience.

Case studies
Innovative practices
Implementation experiences
Lessons from the field

Operational problem-solving
Agency initiatives









EPCL uses a proposal-first process. You do not need to prepare a complete manuscript before receiving an initial editorial decision.




01



Choose a publication and contribution category. Describe your proposed topic, its purpose, and its anticipated contribution.




02



Two editors assigned to the selected publication independently review the proposal for relevance, originality, potential contribution, and suitability.




03



You will receive an approval, denial, or request for modification. Approval is an invitation to develop a manuscript, not a guarantee of publication.




04



Approved contributors receive the universal EPCL manuscript template and submission instructions. The standard development period is 30 days, subject to approved extensions.




05



Editors assess the completed manuscript for quality, clarity, accuracy, relevance, and suitability. Revisions may be requested.




06



Accepted manuscripts proceed to final editorial preparation and publication.





30 Days Standard manuscript development period


2 Editors Assigned to each publication proposal


$0 Submission fee





Approved contributors will receive instructions for developing their full manuscripts.


CONTRIBUTOR RESOURCE

Includes:

Abstract and keyword sections.

Tables, figures, and appendices guidance.

Formatting standard: APA 7th edition · Times New Roman · 12-point · Double-spaced · 1-inch margins.

A few important requirements to understand before submitting your proposal.




Who is eligible to contribute?

EPCL welcomes criminal justice practitioners, researchers, academic faculty, undergraduate and graduate students, administrators, policymakers, retired professionals, and other individuals with relevant knowledge or experience.
Institutional affiliation, academic credentials, and previous publication experience are not prerequisites.



Originality and intellectual property

Contributions should represent original work and must not infringe upon the intellectual property rights of others.
Contributors are responsible for appropriately acknowledging sources. Previously published material, manuscripts under consideration elsewhere, and substantially overlapping submissions must be disclosed.



Professional and ethical standards

Contributors must:

Properly attribute sources and intellectual contributions.
Disclose relevant conflicts of interest.
Identify applicable funding and material support.
Obtain permissions for copyrighted materials.
Protect confidential and personally identifiable information.
Obtain appropriate authorization for research involving human participants when required.

EPCL may request clarification regarding research ethics, institutional approvals, or data permissions.



Manuscript formatting requirements

Full manuscripts must follow APA Publication Manual, Seventh Edition, unless otherwise instructed.

Additional publication-specific instructions may be provided by the editorial team.



How does editorial review work?

Proposals are reviewed by two editors assigned to the selected publication.
Completed manuscripts undergo editorial evaluation for relevance, quality, accuracy, clarity, and suitability.
This process should not be interpreted as external, independent scholarly peer review unless a particular publication explicitly identifies it as such.



Does approval guarantee publication?

No. Proposal approval is an invitation to develop a full manuscript. The completed manuscript must undergo editorial evaluation before a final publication decision is made.



Can I submit to multiple publications?

Contributors should select the publication most closely aligned with their subject matter.
If a proposed contribution could reasonably fit multiple publications, indicate this in the proposal description so the editorial team can consider its placement.

title: Journal Submissions
text:
EPCL accepts proposals across three contribution categories. Contributors should select the category that most closely reflects the purpose and format of their proposed work.


Communicating research and expanding professional knowledge.
This category is intended for contributions that explain, evaluate, synthesize, or communicate research and established knowledge.
Examples include:

Original research articles
Literature reviews
Research summaries
Educational explainers
Program and policy evaluations
Evidence-based practice reviews
Methodological discussions

Contributions should clearly communicate their evidence base and explain the relevance of their findings or subject matter to criminal justice professionals and researchers.



Examining ideas, challenging assumptions, and encouraging professional discussion.
This category provides a platform for examining contemporary issues, discussing competing perspectives, and advancing informed professional dialogue.
Examples include:

Policy analyses
Professional commentary
Opinion essays grounded in evidence
Ethical discussions
Emerging issues in criminal justice
Institutional and organizational critiques
Debates concerning professional practice

Contributions should present a coherent argument, engage meaningfully with relevant evidence or experience, and encourage constructive discussion.



Sharing professional knowledge and practical experience.
This category is intended for practitioners and professionals interested in communicating experiences, describing initiatives, and sharing lessons from the field.
Examples include:

Case studies
Descriptions of innovative practices
Implementation experiences
Lessons learned from professional practice
Interviews with criminal justice professionals
Operational problem-solving approaches
Agency initiatives and program descriptions

Contributions should provide meaningful insights that other professionals can understand, evaluate, or potentially apply in their own organizations.

title: Journal Submissions
text:
EPCL uses a proposal-first submission process. Contributors initially submit a description of their proposed contribution rather than a completed manuscript.
This approach allows editors to evaluate the suitability of a proposed topic before contributors invest time developing a full manuscript.


STEP 01 — PROPOSAL



Select the appropriate journal and contribution category. Provide a proposed title and a description of the topic, purpose, and anticipated contribution.




STEP 02 — EDITORIAL REVIEW



Two editors assigned to the selected publication review the proposal. Editors consider its relevance, originality, potential contribution, and suitability for the publication.




STEP 03 — DECISION



Contributors receive notification of the editorial decision. Proposals may be approved, declined, or returned with a request for modification.
An approved proposal constitutes an invitation to develop a full manuscript. It does not guarantee publication.




STEP 04 — MANUSCRIPT DEVELOPMENT



Approved contributors receive instructions for developing their manuscripts, including the universal EPCL manuscript template and submission deadline.
The standard manuscript development period is 30 days following approval, subject to any extensions approved by the editorial team.




STEP 05 — MANUSCRIPT REVIEW



Submitted manuscripts undergo editorial review. Editors evaluate the quality, clarity, accuracy, relevance, and overall suitability of the manuscript.
Contributors may be asked to revise their work before a final decision is made.




STEP 06 — FINAL DECISION



Accepted manuscripts proceed to editorial preparation and publication. Contributors will be contacted regarding any necessary final revisions and publication details.

title: Journal Submissions
text:
Do I need to be a researcher or academic to submit?

No. EPCL welcomes contributions from practitioners, students, researchers, educators, administrators, and other professionals with relevant knowledge or experience.



Do I need to submit a completed article?

No. EPCL uses a proposal-first process. Initially, you submit a description of your proposed contribution. If approved, you will be invited to develop a full manuscript.



Does proposal approval guarantee publication?

No. Proposal approval is an invitation to develop a manuscript. The completed manuscript must still undergo editorial evaluation before a final publication decision.



Can I submit to more than one EPCL journal?

Contributors should submit proposals to the publication most closely aligned with their subject matter. If a proposed contribution could reasonably fit multiple publications, indicate this in the proposal description so the editorial team can consider its placement.



Can I submit if I have never published before?

Absolutely. EPCL encourages first-time contributors and welcomes individuals interested in sharing knowledge, research, and professional experience.



Will my manuscript undergo peer review?

EPCL uses an editorial review process involving assigned editors. The editorial team evaluates proposals and manuscripts for relevance, quality, accuracy, and suitability. The process should not be interpreted as external, independent scholarly peer review unless a particular publication explicitly identifies it as such.



Is there a submission fee?

There is currently no submission fee.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
The Project
The El Paso Crime Lab is an independent public research project focused on crime, policing, and public safety in El Paso and the Borderland.
The project was established by Matthew Durán to make research and local public safety information more accessible to the public. It brings together academic research, publicly available data, statistical analysis, and other sources of evidence to examine issues affecting the region.
The El Paso Crime Lab is intended as a public-facing resource for research and information. Its purpose is not simply to present statistics, but to provide context, examine evidence, and help readers better understand the complex issues underlying crime and public safety.


The goal is simple: make rigorous research and local evidence easier to find, understand, and use.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
Matthew Durán



Matthew Durán is a criminologist specializing in crime prevention, policing, and public safety research. He is a fourth-year PhD student in the School of Criminology and Criminal Justice at Arizona State University, where he teaches undergraduate and graduate courses on policing and research methods.
His research focuses on applying rigorous quantitative and experimental methods to understand crime patterns and evaluate criminal justice policies and interventions. His work spans policing, victimization, and crime prevention, with an emphasis on translating empirical research into useful insights for policy and practice.
Before beginning his doctoral training, Matthew worked in several criminal justice roles in the El Paso region, including as a crime analyst with the El Paso Police Department, a detention officer with the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office, and a licensed private investigator and fugitive recovery agent.
Matthew established the El Paso Crime Lab as a platform for sharing research, analysis, and public safety information related to El Paso and the broader Borderland.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
Research and Areas of Interest
His work spans across several areas:

Crime prevention and public safety
Policing and police-community relations
Alcohol-impaired driving and traffic safety
Crime and victimization
Criminal justice policy and interventions
Quantitative and experimental research methods
Local crime and public safety data

Selected projects include analyses of alcohol-related crashes and impaired driving outcomes in El Paso, research examining adverse childhood experiences and offending, and the development of data products and research resources for understanding local public safety issues.

title: About the El Paso Crime Lab
text:
Open Access

The El Paso Crime Lab is guided by a commitment to open access and public understanding.
Much of the information used in public safety decision-making is technical, difficult to access, or disconnected from the communities it concerns. This project seeks to make research and local data more accessible by presenting evidence in a clear and transparent way.
Where possible, data sources, methods, limitations, and supporting research are identified so that readers can examine the evidence for themselves.
The project is independent and does not represent or speak on behalf of any law enforcement agency or government organization.

title: Awards Program
text:
The El Paso Crime Lab (EPCL) is proud to announce the inaugural EPCL Public Safety Science Awards, recognizing individuals whose work advances scientific inquiry, strengthens research and evaluation, and promotes the use of data and evidence in public safety.
Good public safety policy begins with good evidence. These awards celebrate the individuals who help make that possible.
SUBMIT A NOMINATION
Nominations open November 1, 2026 — Deadline: December 15, 2026

title: Awards Program
text:
About the Awards
Public safety challenges require more than assumptions and conventional approaches. They require scientific inquiry, reliable data, thoughtful evaluation, and a willingness to continually improve policies and practices.
The EPCL Public Safety Science Awards recognize individuals throughout the El Paso–Borderland region who demonstrate these commitments through their professional work, research, education, or community contributions.
Whether conducting research, improving organizational data systems, evaluating programs, or helping translate scientific findings into practice, award recipients exemplify the importance of evidence-informed public safety.

title: Awards Program
text:
2026 Award Categories
The inaugural awards recognize contributions across six categories.


01. Dedication to Scientific Inquiry Award
Recognizes an individual who demonstrates exceptional dedication, initiative, and perseverance in pursuing scientific inquiry and advancing research-informed approaches to public safety.
This award recognizes curiosity, intellectual commitment, and the pursuit of scientific knowledge, including research proposals and projects that may still be in development.


02. Advancing Program Evaluation Award
Recognizes an individual who strengthens the ability to assess and improve programs through better data collection, measurement, evaluation systems, and organizational evaluation capacity.


03. Science in Action Award
Recognizes an individual who translates research, scientific knowledge, or data into practical improvements in public safety policies, programs, or practices.


04. Evidence-Based Practice Advancement Award
Recognizes an individual who promotes the use of scientific research and credible evidence in public safety policies, procedures, and practices.


05. Scientific Leadership Award
Recognizes an individual who demonstrates leadership in advancing scientific thinking, research collaboration, and evidence-informed decision-making within an organization or community.


06. Emerging Researcher Award
Recognizes a student or early-career professional demonstrating exceptional promise, initiative, or contribution to research and the science of public safety.

title: Awards Program
text:
Eligibility Requirements
To be considered for a 2026 EPCL Public Safety Science Award, nominees must meet the following requirements:

Geographic eligibility: Nominees must live, work, study, or conduct relevant professional or community activities within the El Paso–Borderland region.
2026 contributions: The work or contributions being recognized must have occurred between January 1 and December 31, 2026.
Individual recognition: Awards recognize individuals rather than organizations, agencies, or institutions.
Relevant contributions: Nominees must demonstrate contributions related to scientific inquiry, research, data, program evaluation, evidence-informed policy, or public safety practice.
Open professional eligibility: Students, researchers, analysts, public safety professionals, educators, administrators, program managers, and community members are welcome.

Formal research credentials, academic publications, and demonstrated program effectiveness are not required. Contributions may include foundational work such as improving data collection, developing measurement systems, establishing evaluation practices, or advancing research initiatives.

title: Awards Program
text:
Nomination Process
Nominations are open to the public. Anyone may nominate an eligible individual, including nominating themselves.
How to nominate:

Review the six award categories.
Select the category that best reflects the nominee’s contributions.
Complete the online nomination form.
Describe the nominee’s work and provide an example of their contribution.

You may submit multiple nominations for different individuals or award categories. Please submit a separate nomination for each individual and category.
NOMINATE SOMEONE TODAY

title: Awards Program
text:
Selection and Recognition
Nominations will be reviewed by the El Paso Crime Lab and an awards selection committee. Submissions will be evaluated based on the nominee’s contributions, commitment to scientific inquiry, advancement of evidence-informed approaches, and relevance to the award category.
Recipients will be notified privately before the public announcement.
Award recipients will receive formal recognition from the El Paso Crime Lab, including an official award certificate and acknowledgment through EPCL communication channels.

The Courts Journal

Our approach
EPCL Publications seeks to bridge the gap between research and practice.
We welcome contributions that explain research, examine professional experiences, evaluate public safety initiatives, and translate evidence into useful knowledge.
Our goal is not simply to produce more publications. It is to encourage better questions, stronger evidence, and more informed decisions.

For Authors
EPCL Publications welcomes contributions from researchers, practitioners, and community contributors interested in advancing the science of public safety.

Contribution categories
Research & Education
Research articles, research briefs, literature reviews, educational explainers, evidence summaries, and theoretical discussions.
Perspectives & Debate
Opinion pieces, professional reflections, arguments, critiques, and commentary on issues affecting public safety and the justice system.
Practice & Experience
Lessons learned, professional experiences, practical guides, case studies, and descriptions of initiatives and programs.


Publication process

Proposal submission. Authors submit a brief description of their proposed contribution.
Initial editorial assessment. The editorial team evaluates the proposal for relevance and suitability.
Invitation to develop. Selected proposals receive an invitation to prepare a full manuscript.
Manuscript submission. Authors submit their completed contributions.
Editorial review. The manuscript is reviewed, with revisions requested when appropriate.
Final decision. The editorial team communicates an acceptance or rejection decision.
Production and publication. Accepted contributions are edited, formatted, and published.

Editorial Policies
EPCL Publications is committed to producing work that is accurate, relevant, transparent, and useful to its intended audiences.

Editorial independence
Editorial decisions should be based on the relevance, quality, and suitability of submitted work.


Review process
Submissions are subject to editorial assessment. The specific review process may vary according to contribution type and journal.


Publication ethics
Authors are expected to present their work accurately, acknowledge relevant sources, and disclose potential conflicts of interest.


Conflicts of interest
Authors and editors should disclose relationships or interests that could reasonably be perceived as influencing the work or editorial process.


Corrections and retractions
EPCL Publications may issue corrections, clarifications, or retractions when necessary to maintain the accuracy and integrity of its publications.


Transparency
EPCL aims to communicate its editorial procedures and provide aggregate information about publication activity and editorial decision times.

The El Paso Crime Lab publishes research, professional knowledge, and accessible educational resources that advance the science of public safety in the Borderland. Each journal serves a distinct audience and area of the criminal justice system.

The Community Safety Journal
The Community Safety Journal makes research and public safety knowledge accessible to community members, local organizations, policymakers, and other interested readers.
Contributions may examine local public safety concerns, community experiences, criminal justice policy, prevention initiatives, and research findings with practical implications for the Borderland. The journal prioritizes accessible writing and clear explanations that help readers understand complex issues.


The Police Journal
The Police Journal advances research-informed policing by connecting criminological research, professional experience, and practical knowledge.
Contributions may address police organizations, patrol operations, problem-oriented policing, crime analysis, officer development, organizational leadership, program evaluation, and emerging issues in law enforcement. The journal welcomes research briefs, educational explainers, professional perspectives, and evaluations of policing strategies.


The Corrections Journal
The Corrections Journal examines the institutions, practices, and policies that shape correctional systems.
Contributions may address jails, prisons, community corrections, institutional safety, rehabilitation, reentry, correctional personnel, and organizational management. The journal emphasizes evidence-informed approaches to improving correctional practice and outcomes.


The Courts Journal
The Courts Journal explores the administration, operation, and impact of courts and related justice institutions.
Contributions may address court administration, case processing, pretrial practices, sentencing, access to justice, judicial policy, and the experiences of individuals navigating the court system. The journal encourages research and practical perspectives that support effective, fair, and informed justice processes.



Have knowledge or experience to share? We welcome contributions from researchers, public safety professionals, students, and community members.

Three types of contributions



Research & Education
Explain research, share findings, or teach readers about a topic.


Perspectives & Debate
Share an informed opinion or offer a different way to think about an issue.


Practice & Experience
Share practical advice, professional experiences, or lessons learned.



How to get published

Submit a short proposal describing your idea.
If approved, write and submit your article.
Editors review your article and may ask for changes.
If accepted, your article is prepared for publication.

You do not need a finished article to submit a proposal.

EPCL Publications seeks to maintain transparent and consistent editorial practices. The following policies describe the principles guiding publication decisions and the handling of submitted work.

Editorial Independence
Publication decisions are based on the relevance, quality, and suitability of contributions. Authors’ professional affiliations and institutional positions do not guarantee acceptance.


Editorial Review
All submissions undergo editorial assessment. Additional review may be requested depending on the nature, scope, and intended contribution of the manuscript.


Publication Ethics
Authors are responsible for the accuracy and integrity of their submissions, appropriate acknowledgment of sources, and disclosure of relevant conflicts of interest.


Conflicts of Interest
Authors and editors should disclose relationships or interests that could reasonably be perceived as influencing the preparation, review, or publication of a contribution.


Corrections and Retractions
EPCL may issue corrections, expressions of concern, or retractions when necessary to maintain the accuracy and integrity of its publications.


Copyright and Permissions
Publication and reuse conditions will be communicated to contributors during the submission and acceptance process.
